aliases.reason: The slash-free spelling used throughout RFC text and in the group name; the desc indexes "s/mime" as one word (the `/` stays inside the token), and matching is prefix-directional, so typing SMIME finds nothing today.

notes: "S/MIME" itself is already reachable via the desc word s/mime, so it is redundant. Predecessor/competitor mail-security schemes (PEM, MOSS, PGP/OpenPGP) are different technologies, not other names for S/MIME, and PEM and openpgp already have their own tags. Components such as SignedData, EnvelopedData and triple-wrapping are sub-features and belong to full-text search; the underlying syntax layer is the parent tag cms.

PEM has essentially one name, and typing "PEM", "privacy", "enhanced" or "mail" already lands on the tag via the desc, so nothing survives rule 4. Two things considered and rejected: (1) "MOSS" (MIME Object Security Services, RFC 1848) is PEM's MIME-based successor but is a distinct technology, not another name for PEM, so rule 1 excludes it; it is too thin a body of work to propose as its own tag. (2) "PEM" is also widely used today for the textual certificate/key encoding (RFC 7468, "PEM format"), which readers may be searching for; that is a naming collision rather than an alias, and such queries arguably belong nearer `x509`/`pki` — worth a human decision but not something to encode in this field.

multiword.reason: Variant name for EST over secure CoAP (RFC 9148); the hyphen splits it into two tokens so it cannot be matched as a single query today, but readers do type it as the name of this protocol variant.

notes: The desc word `est` already makes the tag findable by its only real name, so no plain alias survives rule 4. `enrollment` and `transport` are likewise already in the desc (and `transport` is another tag's id). Related certificate-management protocols such as CMC (RFC 5272), SCEP (RFC 8894) and SZTP/BRSKI are different technologies, not other names for EST, so they are excluded by rule 1 — BRSKI already has its own tag (`brski`) and CMP has `cmp`. `coaps` alone was rejected: it names CoAP over DTLS, not EST.

MLS has only one name; the tag id, the working group name and the expansion in the desc all coincide, and 'Messaging Layer Security' is already indexed word by word in the desc so no spelled-out form is needed. TreeKEM, MLSPlaintext/MLSCiphertext, the ratchet tree and the Delivery Service are components or sub-features of MLS (rule 2), not other names for it. Signal/Double Ratchet, OTR and Sender Keys are different group-messaging technologies (rule 1), not aliases; the generic term 'end-to-end encryption' is area vocabulary (rule 3). 'messaging' and 'instant-messaging' are existing tag ids (rule 5).

aliases.reason: CMS is the IETF continuation of RSA's PKCS #7 syntax; the two names denote the same message syntax and readers routinely type the older name. Not findable in the desc, and it is a single indexed token since '#' stays inside a word.
Unseparated spelling of the same predecessor name, as it appears in ASN.1 module and OID identifiers (e.g. id-pkcs7 / pkcs-7) in RFC text; a reader is as likely to type this form as PKCS#7.

multiword.reason: The most common spelling in RFC titles and prose (RFC 2315), but it is two tokens so the current whole-query search cannot find it; worth enabling once multi-word aliases are searchable.

notes: S/MIME and CMC/certificate-management terms were considered and rejected: s-mime is already a child tag (rule 5), and CMC is a separate protocol built on CMS rather than another name for it. Content types such as SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData are components of the syntax (rule 2), not alternative names. 'PKCS' alone was not proposed because it names the whole PKCS family, most of which belongs elsewhere (pki, x509).

aliases.reason: The original and still most common name for the technology; the desc indexes only 'openpgp', 'open', 'pretty', 'good', 'privacy', and none of those words starts with 'pgp', so typing PGP finds nothing today. Present in `match`, but `match` is never searched.
The dominant implementation name, widely used informally to mean OpenPGP itself and appearing in RFC text; a reader typing it wants this tag and nothing in the desc makes it reachable.

notes: Considered and rejected: 'GPG' (same intent as GnuPG but I am less confident it occurs as a standalone token in RFC text — worth adding if a corpus check confirms it); 'PGP/MIME' and 'OpenPGP Web Key Directory'/'WKD' (components/bindings of the subject, rule 2); 'keyserver', 'key', 'signature', 'encryption' (generic vocabulary, rule 3); 'S/MIME' (a different technology with its own tag `s-mime`, rule 1/5). 'Pretty Good Privacy' needs no multiword entry since 'pretty', 'good' and 'privacy' are each already indexed from the desc.

SASL has exactly one name, and its expansion (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) is already in the desc as ordinary whole words, so 'simple', 'authentication' and 'security' all reach the tag today. Named SASL mechanisms (PLAIN, ANONYMOUS, EXTERNAL, CRAM-MD5, DIGEST-MD5, SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER, GS2) are components/instances of the framework, not other names for it, so rule 2 excludes them from aliases; SASL is a single framework rather than a category standing in for missing tags, so it takes no covers either. GS2 and the GSSAPI bridge mechanisms belong with the existing `gssapi` tag; SCRAM is the only mechanism with enough standalone RFC presence to ever merit its own tag, but it is not substantial enough to propose here.
PANA has one name; the acronym and its expansion are both in the desc and already searchable. Related terms like EAP, AAA and RADIUS are different technologies with their own tags (rule 1 / rule 5).

aliases.reason: Standard short form of Kerberos Version 5 used throughout RFC text (krb5.conf, krb5 mechanism names, Kerberos V5 spec RFC 4120); names the same system, and the desc words the/kerberos/authentication/system do not make it findable.

notes: Deliberately excluded: KDC, TGT, TGS, AS-REQ, PKINIT, PA-DATA are components or sub-features of Kerberos (rule 2). GSS-API and SPNEGO are a different technology with their own home — the existing `gssapi` tag (rules 1 and 5). KINK (Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys) is a distinct key-management protocol, not another name for Kerberos, even though the kink WG is listed in this tag's groups; it is small enough that it does not obviously merit its own tag, so it is left to full-text search rather than claimed here. `krb` alone was considered and dropped: it is not confidently attested as a standalone whole word in RFC text (it appears mainly as a prefix in message-type names like KRB_AP_REQ), and an unattested term would only earn a rejection.

The tag has essentially one name plus one acronym, and both are already reachable. 'HOKEY' is the tag id itself and also a desc word; 'ERP' appears in the desc as '(ERP)' and parentheses split, so the indexed word is exactly 'erp' and a reader typing ERP lands here today (rule 4). 'Handover' and 'keying' are likewise plain desc words. Considered and rejected: EMSK, DSRK, rRK/rMSK and ERX are key-hierarchy components or sub-features of ERP, not other names for it (rule 2). 'reauthentication' (unhyphenated) would not match the desc, which indexes 're' and 'authentication' separately, but it is generic vocabulary rather than a name for this protocol, and rule 3 outranks rule 4 — full-text search already serves it. AAA/EAP handover terms such as 'fast re-authentication' belong to the parent 'eap' tag, not here. No covers list: this names a single technology, not a category.

aliases.reason: Trusted Network Connect, the TCG framework name for the same endpoint-posture-assessment technology that the IETF NEA work adopted (PA-TNC/PB-TNC/PT-EAP carry the name); readers commonly type TNC for this subject and the desc contains no word starting with 'tnc'.

notes: PA-TNC, PB-TNC, PT-TLS and PT-EAP are the individual protocols within the NEA architecture (rule 2 components), so they are not listed. NAC (Network Access Control) is a broader, different access-control notion rather than another name for endpoint posture assessment, so it is excluded under rule 1; posture-collection/evaluation work of the later SACM kind belongs to the existing `sacm` tag. 'endpoint', 'assessment' and 'posture' are all already reachable by searching the desc.

SACM has only one name: the acronym is the tag id and the expansion 'security automation and continuous monitoring' is fully in the desc, where 'security', 'automation', 'continuous' and 'monitoring' are each independently searchable whole words. Candidates considered and rejected: SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) is a separate NIST specification suite that SACM documents reference, not another name for SACM — rule 1; it appears in too few RFCs to suggest as its own tag. EPCP / Endpoint Posture Collection Protocol and the SACM information model/architecture pieces are components of the work, not synonyms — rule 2. 'endpoint posture assessment' and 'posture' belong with the existing `nea` tag (Network Endpoint Assessment), which is a sibling here, rather than with SACM. 'continuous monitoring' alone is already reachable via the desc and is multi-word besides. SACM names a single work area, not a category, so it has no `covers`.

AAA has no genuine synonym or predecessor name: the only alternate form is the spelled-out expansion 'Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting', and each of those words is already indexed from the desc (and is generic vocabulary besides), so nothing survives rule 3/rule 4. The concrete AAA protocols a reader might type — RADIUS, Diameter, TACACS(+) — all have their own tags (they are this tag's children), so rule 6's second condition fails and they belong in neither `aliases` nor `covers`; likewise 'accounting' as a bare word is generic and already reachable. Related terms such as NAS, NAI, and Diameter application names (NASREQ, CCA) are components/sub-features and belong to full-text search. Neighbouring but distinct technologies route to their own tags: EAP -> `eap`, PANA -> `pana`, network access authorization policy -> `policy-management`.

Diameter has exactly one name and the desc word `diameter` already makes it findable. RADIUS and TACACS are different protocols with their own tags (rules 1 and 5), not aliases, even though Diameter is RADIUS's successor. `DIME` is the working group name and does appear in RFC text, but it is used to denote the WG/mailing list rather than as a name for the protocol itself, so I did not propose it; if the maintainers judge that readers do type DIME expecting the protocol, it would be the only plausible candidate here. Components and extensions such as Diameter applications, AVPs, CER/CEA, or Diameter-SIP are sub-features (rule 2) and belong to full-text search.

aliases.reason: Informal/vendor name for RADIUS over TLS (used as such in RFC 6614 and related documents); it denotes the RADIUS protocol itself carried over a secure transport rather than a different protocol, and it is not findable today since neither the tag name nor the desc contains the string.

notes: Deliberately excluded: `diameter` and `tacacs` are sibling tags (different technologies, rule 1); NASREQ, RADEXT and ROAMOPS are working-group names that readers do not use as names for the protocol itself; CoA, Disconnect-Message, VSA, NAS and AVP are components/sub-features of RADIUS (rule 2). 'Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service' is already word-indexed in the desc, so its component words (remote, authentication, dial-in, user, service) are reachable.

The desc already contains "JWT" and "JSON", "Web", "Token", so both the acronym and the expansion are findable today. Related terms are either components or different technologies: JWS, JWE and JWK are separate JOSE constructs belonging under the existing `jose` tag, not other names for JWT; `jwt` profiles such as PoP or DPoP are sub-features. No superseded or vendor name for JWT exists in RFC text.

EAP has exactly one name, and it is the first word of the desc, so a reader typing EAP or extensible already lands here. Considered and rejected: (a) EAP method names -- EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS, PEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA, EAP-pwd, EAP-PSK, EAP-NOOB -- these are sub-protocols/instances within EAP, so rule 2 applies; the tag is a single technology (kind: technology) rather than a category standing in for unrelated things, so it takes no `covers` list, and full-text search already finds these names well. (b) 802.1X and EAPOL -- port-based network access control and the LAN encapsulation are different technologies that merely carry EAP, so rule 1 applies; neither looks substantial enough here to propose as its own tag without wider review. (c) EMU and the eap WG name -- EMU (EAP Method Update) is a working-group name readers are unlikely to type meaning the protocol itself, unlike SPRING->segment-routing, and `eap` as a WG name is already the tag id. (d) Generic terms such as authentication, supplicant and authenticator belong to full-text search, and `authentication` is another tag's id (rule 5).

JOSE has no genuine synonyms or predecessor names; the tag name is the working group name and the technology name. JWS, JWE and JWK are sub-specifications (rule 2) and are in any case already whole words in the desc, so they are reachable today. JWA (JSON Web Algorithms) is likewise a component of the family, not another name for it, so it is not proposed. JWT has its own tag (rule 5) and readers typing it should land there. 'JavaScript' is already indexed from the desc expansion.

The desc already indexes `gnap` plus `grant`, `negotiation`, `authorization`, so the tag's own name and its expansion are reachable today. GNAP has no superseded or variant name of its own: it is a distinct protocol, not a version of OAuth, so `oauth` (the parent, and an existing tag anyway under rule 5) must not be listed here. Candidate historical names were considered and dropped: `TxAuth` (the pre-chartering BoF/mailing-list name) and `XYZ` / `XAuth` (the two individual draft proposals GNAP was built from) are at best mentioned in acknowledgement or history prose, and I am not confident enough that they occur as searchable terms in published RFC text to risk a corpus rejection; `XYZ` would in any case be a poor search token. `RAR`, `GNAP resource servers`, `grant request`, `access token` and similar are components or generic vocabulary (rules 2-3). This is a single technology, so it has no `covers`.

covers.reason: The Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation Mechanism (RFC 2478, RFC 4178, RFC 4559) is a GSS-API mechanism with no tag of its own; the desc explicitly scopes this tag to GSS-API "and its mechanisms", so a reader typing SPNEGO has nowhere better to land. Not an alias: it is a distinct mechanism, not another name for GSS-API itself.
Simple Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism (RFC 2025, RFC 2847) — a named GSS-API mechanism with no tag of its own, in scope per "and its mechanisms", and not findable from the desc.
Low Infrastructure Public Key mechanism layered over SPKM (RFC 2847) — a GSS-API mechanism with no tag of its own and no presence in the desc.

missing_tag_candidates.reason: Negotiation mechanism with its own RFC lineage (2478, 4178) plus the HTTP Negotiate binding (4559, and its successors in HTTP auth work); it spans GSS-API, Kerberos and HTTP authentication, so it may warrant a tag rather than sitting permanently under gssapi's covers.

notes: No aliases proposed. "GSS" and "gssapi" are already reachable: the desc splits "GSS-API" on the hyphen into the indexed words `gss` and `api`, and the tag id `gssapi` is itself matched by the prefix query `gss`, so both land the reader here today. The hyphenated form "GSS-API" as typed may not match any single indexed word, but it is the tag's own name rather than a variant name, so it is a search-tokenisation issue rather than an alias. GSS-KRB5 / the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism belongs to the existing `kerberos` tag, not here (rule 5 also bars it as a near-duplicate route). ABFAB / GSS-EAP work belongs with `federated-authentication` and `eap`. The working group names CAT and KITTEN were considered under the SPRING->segment-routing precedent and rejected: "CAT" is generic and ambiguous, and neither is used in RFC text as a name for the technology itself, so both would risk corpus rejection and false hits.

aliases.reason: Closed-up version form of the tag's own name, common in prose and identifiers; the desc word `oauth` does not start with `oauth2`, so a reader typing OAuth2 finds nothing today.

notes: Deliberately excluded: PKCE, DPoP, bearer token, token introspection and device flow are extensions/components of OAuth (rule 2), not other names for it. OpenID Connect / OIDC is a distinct identity layer built on top of OAuth (rule 1) and is not an alias; it also has little RFC-series presence, so I am not proposing it as a missing tag. JWT and GNAP are existing tags (rule 5). 'authorization' alone is generic vocabulary and is already its own tag.

multiword.reason: The expanded name of COSE; it is in the desc, but as separate words a reader typing the whole phrase cannot match it today since the search never splits a query. Worth holding until multi-word search exists.

missing_tag_candidates.reason: CBOR Web Token (RFC 8392) is a distinct technology built on COSE, not another name for it — the CBOR counterpart of JWT, which already has its own tag. Readers typing CWT currently have no good landing spot; it is not an alias of cose.

notes: COSE has essentially one name. 'CBOR' alone is already reachable: the desc word '(cbor' indexes as 'cbor' and a query of 'cbor' matches it, so it would be redundant even if it were a name for this tag rather than the underlying data format. COSE_Key, COSE_Sign1, COSE_Encrypt and the algorithm registry entries are components/sub-features (rule 2). OSCORE and EDHOC use COSE but have their own tags (rule 5 / rule 1). JOSE is the JSON-based sibling family, a different technology with its own tag.

SCIM has one name, and the desc already indexes `scim`, so typing it lands correctly today. The original expansion "Simple Cloud Identity Management" (pre-2.0) is a genuine predecessor name but is multi-word, has no distinctive single token to search on, and appears rarely in RFC text; not worth queueing. Provisioning-adjacent terms were considered and rejected: SPML (OASIS Service Provisioning Markup Language) is a different technology, not a former name for SCIM (rule 1), and `provisioning` is generic vocabulary better served by full-text search (rule 3). Filter/PATCH/ServiceProviderConfig-style terms are components of the protocol (rule 2). Readers arriving from the identity side are served by the existing `federated-authentication`, `oauth` and `directory-services` tags.

aliases.reason: Cisco's 'extended TACACS' variant, named in the protocol's history (e.g. RFC 1492's extended TACACS and the background section of the TACACS+ spec); a reader typing XTACACS means this tag, and the desc word 'tacacs' does not start with 'xtacacs' so it is not findable today.

notes: TACACS+ is already reachable: '+' stays inside the indexed word, so the desc word 'tacacs+' matches the query 'tacacs+' (and 'tacacs' matches both desc words), making it redundant under rule 4. 'Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System' and its Plus form are multi-word and each significant word is already in the desc, so nothing is needed under multiword. RADIUS and Diameter are sibling AAA protocols, not other names for TACACS, so they are excluded by rule 1.

aliases.reason: Standard abbreviation of Security Event Token (RFC 8417) and the form used throughout the delivery specs (RFC 8935/8936); the desc's indexed words are security/event/tokens/delivery, none of which start with 'set', so a reader typing SET lands nowhere today. Note it is ambiguous with the historical Secure Electronic Transaction work, so if a corpus check shows the hits dominated by that sense it is fair to drop.

notes: Considered and rejected: SSE (Shared Signals and Events), CAEP and RISC are OpenID Foundation profiles built on SETs rather than other names for this tag's subject, and are unlikely to appear in RFC text; 'seceventtoken' is a WG/list handle, not a term a reader would type. 'token' and 'delivery' are already reachable via the desc. JWT-related terms belong to the existing `jwt` tag.

RSA has essentially one name, and the desc already indexes rivest, shamir and adleman as separate words (punctuation splits), so the expanded name is reachable. Considered and rejected: PKCS#1 (the specification defining RSA schemes, a component/standard rather than another name for the algorithm — parallel to the PKCS -> pki example in rule 2); RSASSA-PSS, RSAES-OAEP, RSA-PSS, RSA-OAEP (padding/signature schemes within RSA, sub-features under rule 2 — and since '-' splits words, their leading 'RSA' token is matched by the tag name anyway); 'public-key' (generic vocabulary, rule 3, and better served by the existing pki and cryptography tags).

aliases.reason: The original/competition name of the cipher selected as AES; denotes the exact same block cipher, appears in real RFC text (e.g. AES/Rijndael discussions in CMS and TLS cipher documents), and is not reachable from the desc, which never contains the word.

notes: Nothing else qualifies. Mode names (GCM, CCM, CBC, CTR, GCM-SIV, KW/AESKW) are sub-features of "and its modes" under rule 2, not other names for AES. Other ciphers and algorithms (DES/3DES, ChaCha20, Camellia, SHA, RSA) are different technologies under rule 1, and most already have sibling tags (des, chacha20, sha, rsa). Key-length forms such as AES-128/AES-256 are hyphenated, so the search would split neither the query nor usefully match them, and the desc word "aes" already lands a reader typing AES on this tag. "Advanced" and "Encryption" are each already whole words in the desc, so the spelled-out name is redundant.

aliases.reason: Predecessor cipher of the same family that this tag's match expression explicitly covers; it appears in the tag's match but match is never searched, and the desc word 'chacha20' does not make 'salsa20' findable.

notes: Poly1305 is deliberately omitted: it is a whole word in the desc ('ChaCha20 and Poly1305'), so typing poly1305 already lands on this tag. 'ChaCha' alone is likewise redundant, since the indexed desc word 'chacha20' starts with that query. XChaCha20 was considered and dropped for lack of confident RFC-corpus occurrence. AES-GCM, GCM and other AEAD constructions are different technologies and belong to aes, not here.

aliases.reason: Working group name (Application Bridging for Federated Authentication Beyond the Web) listed in this tag's groups; readers routinely use the WG acronym for the technology itself, and it is not reachable from the desc.

Morphological variant of the tag's own name, denoting the same thing. Not reachable today: the desc word is 'federated', and matching is directional, so 'federated' does not start with the query 'federation'.

covers.reason: The dominant cross-domain federated authentication framework and the primary term in this tag's match expression, but there is no 'saml' tag, so a reader typing SAML has nowhere better to land. It is a distinct framework rather than another name for the tag, so it belongs in covers, not aliases.

missing_tag_candidates.reason: Substantial enough body of work (assertions, bindings, SAML/SASL and SAML/EAP bridging, metadata) that it could justify its own tag under security; listed in covers in the meantime.

notes: Deliberately excluded: GSS-EAP, trust router and assertion/attribute terms are components of ABFAB rather than other names for the tag (rule 2). 'SSO'/'single sign-on' was considered and dropped: single sign-on is a broader, not necessarily cross-domain, property and also squarely covers oauth and kerberos, so it would produce a confidently wrong single hit; full-text search serves it better. 'eduroam' is a deployed RADIUS/EAP roaming federation and fits aaa/radius/eap at least as well as this tag, so I have not claimed it here. 'Moonshot' (the project name behind ABFAB) was omitted as too sparsely attested in RFC text to be confident. 'vectors of trust' is in match but is multi-word and names one specific specification rather than this tag.

aliases.reason: Standard written form of Triple-DES, extremely common in RFC cipher suite and algorithm text (e.g. 3des-cbc in SSH, TLS ciphersuites). The desc contains only 'triple-des', which splits into 'triple' and 'des', so no desc word starts with '3des' and a reader typing 3DES finds nothing today.

Triple Data Encryption Algorithm, the NIST/ANSI name for Triple-DES, used alongside 'Triple DES' in RFC text such as the DES security-implications and CMS algorithm documents. Not derivable from any desc word.

notes: 'DES-EDE3', 'des-cbc', 'des-ede3-cbc' and similar are keying/mode names for the same cipher rather than alternative names for it, and they are hyphenated so they would not survive whole-word search; left out. 'DEA' (Data Encryption Algorithm) is a genuine alternate name for DES but is a rare, highly ambiguous three-letter string in RFC text, so I did not propose it. Related historic ciphers (DESX, IDEA, RC2, Skipjack, Blowfish) are different technologies and are excluded by rule 1; none seemed substantial enough in the RFC series to propose as new tags. Typing 'triple' already reaches this tag via the desc word, so no multiword entry is needed.

aliases.reason: Name of the Diffie-Hellman function defined on Curve25519 (RFC 7748, RFC 8446); the same technology under its function name, and not reachable today since the desc word 'curve25519' does not start with 'x25519'. Already in `match`, but `match` is never searched.
The Curve448 counterpart of X25519, named throughout RFC 7748/8446; same technology, and unreachable from the desc word 'curve448'.
Informal name for Curve448 (Ed448-Goldilocks) used in RFC 7748 and RFC 8032; a variant name for the same curve, not findable from the desc.

notes: Ed25519 and Ed448 are deliberately excluded: they name the signature schemes, which belong to the sibling tag `eddsa`, not to the curve tag. Generic terms like ECDH and ECC are area vocabulary and belong to the parent `elliptic-curve` / full-text search.

aliases.reason: The EdDSA instantiation over edwards25519 — a variant/parameter-set name for the same signature algorithm (cf. NFSv4 -> nfs), used far more often in RFC text than the bare name EdDSA. Not reachable today: the desc indexes only eddsa/edwards/curve/digital/signature/algorithm, none of which start with 'ed25519', and `match` is never searched.
The other EdDSA instantiation (over edwards448) — same algorithm, variant name. Not findable from the desc for the same reason; appears throughout RFC 8032 and its users.

notes: Ed25519 is treated as a variant name rather than a `covers` instance because EdDSA names one algorithm with two defined parameter sets, not a category of distinct technologies. Ed25519 may legitimately also be searched toward the sibling `curve25519` tag, since edwards25519 and X25519/Curve25519 are the signature and key-agreement faces of the same curve family; if `curve25519` is scoped to the curve itself rather than to X25519 key exchange, listing Ed25519 there as well would be reasonable. Sub-modes PureEdDSA and HashEdDSA (Ed25519ph, Ed25519ctx, Ed448ph) are excluded as sub-features under rule 2.

covers.reason: The desc explicitly scopes this tag to MD4, but the desc's indexed word is `md2/md4` (the `/` stays inside the word), so typing MD4 alone lands nowhere today. MD4 is a distinct algorithm from MD5 rather than another name for it, and no `md4` tag exists, so it belongs in `covers` rather than `aliases`.

notes: MD2 needs no entry: the desc word `md2/md4` starts with `md2`, so a reader typing MD2 already reaches this tag. The tag name itself is the only name MD5 has; `message digest` and `Message Digest 5` are already reachable via the desc words `message`/`digest`/`digests`. MD4 and MD2 are deliberately folded into this tag by the desc and are historical enough that neither looks worth its own tag, so nothing is queued under missing_tag_candidates. Sibling digests (SHA-1, SHA-2) stay out under rule 1 — `sha` exists; HMAC-MD5 constructions belong to the existing `hmac` tag.

aliases.reason: Standard abbreviation of "elliptic curve cryptography" — another name for the same subject. The desc indexes only the whole words "elliptic", "curve" and "cryptography" (the hyphen in "Elliptic-Curve" splits), so typing ECC lands nowhere today. Appears spelled out as ECC throughout RFC crypto text (e.g. RFC 6090, RFC 5639).

covers.reason: The elliptic-curve signature algorithm: a distinct thing from ECC-in-general, but no `ecdsa` tag exists and the tag's own `match` already pulls these RFCs in, so this tag is where an ECDSA reader should land. Not reachable from the desc.

The elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement scheme; no tag of its own, already inside this tag's `match`, and nothing in the desc makes it findable. Instance of the category, not another name for it.
The ephemeral form, ubiquitous in TLS cipher-suite names; matching is prefix-directional so the word `ecdh` does not make `ECDHE` findable. Same standing as ECDH: no better tag exists.

No alias survives. 'ARPA' and 'ARPA network' are already reachable: the desc word 'arpanet' starts with the query 'arpa', so typing ARPA lands here today (rule 4). 'IMP'/'IMPs', '1822' and 'host-IMP' are components of the ARPANET (its packet switches and the BBN 1822 host-to-IMP interface), not other names for the network, so rule 2 keeps them out of aliases; they are correctly carried in `match`, which is where they do their work. 'DARPA' names the agency, not the network, and 'ARPA Internet' is both multiword and a different thing (the early Internet, not the ARPANET itself). 'MILNET' and 'CSNET' are distinct networks rather than variant names, and `arpanet` names one network rather than a category, so it has no `covers`; neither looks substantial enough in the corpus to warrant its own tag, so I have not queued them. The children ncp, supdup, rje and network-graphics are existing tag ids and excluded by rule 5.

No confident aliases. The tag's own name is the only name for it, and a reader typing "graphics" or "graphic" already lands here via the desc word `graphics` (prefix match also catches "graphic"). Considered and rejected: "NGP"/"NGG" (Network Graphics Protocol / Network Graphics Group) — plausible-looking expansions of the ARPANET-era graphics RFCs, but I am not confident either acronym actually appears as a standalone token in RFC text, and the guidance is explicit that an invented acronym only costs a rejection. "raster", "vector", "display", "plotting" are generic vocabulary (rule 3) and belong to full-text search. Later image formats such as PNG, GIF and JPEG were rejected under rule 1: they are different technologies from the ARPANET-era network graphics protocols this tag sits under (path arpanet/network-graphics), and mapping them here would produce a confidently wrong hit for a reader looking for RFC 2083 and friends; if the vocabulary ever wants those, they want their own tag rather than an alias here, so I have deliberately not filed them as missing_tag_candidates for this tag either.
